newsitem.title: USA: NIH weighs into marijuana health debate.
newsitem.headline: NIH weighs into marijuana health debate.

text.p: The National Institutes of Health on Wednesday began exploring how to bring scientific research to bear in the raging controversy over the medical use of marijuana.

The NIH started a two-day workshop, in which outside experts summarized what is known and what has yet to be learned about marijuana's possible benefits for people with AIDS, cancer, multiple sclerosis or other serious diseases.
The experts also discussed some of the difficulties in conducting clinical trials, noting for instance that it would be hard to develop a harmless placebo for a "joint."

The NIH workshop, which was interrupted by a small but vocal group of demonstrators favouring medical use of marijuana, will conclude Thursday and a panel of outside advisers will probably take a month or so to complete its recommendations on what type of marijuana-related research the NIH might conduct or support.

Medical use of marijuana has been studied and debated for decades, but it has come to the fore again since voters in California and Arizona last November approved initiatives to make it available to patients.

The Clinton administration has come down hard against medical marijuana, threatening to penalise any doctors that incorporate it in their practice. Under federal law, marijuana is illegal and has no approved clinical use.

Protesters and some advocacy groups demanded that the NIH immediately allow seriously ill people to get marijuana under experimental projects or through "compassionate access" programmes that would allow patients to get drugs that have not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

"Our focus is on the state of the science," Dr. Alan Leshner, director of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, said as he opened the conference, which some protesters derided as a political show and not a scientific session.

Leshner said that the NIH was "quite open" to supporting research on marijuana and "would welcome proposals" from outside scientists. Such grant applications would go through the usual peer review evaluation at NIH.

A synthetic form of THC, or delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the active ingredient of marijuana, has been available in pill form for several years and can be legally prescribed for cancer patients and for AIDS patients suffering from "wasting syndrome" in which they lose dangerous amounts of weight.

But that drug is not absorbed well by all patients, particularly those with gastrointestinal problems. Several studies have found that people reported more relief from smoking marijuana than taking the pill.
Although some studies have shown that marijuana can help control nausea in cancer patients, they remain controversial.
Some doctors say that marijuana can provide significant relief to terminally ill patients.

For instance, New England Journal of Medicine editor Dr. Jerome Kassirer recently wrote, "I believe that a federal policy that prohibits physicians from alleviating suffering by prescribing marijuana for seriously ill patients is misguided, heavy-handed and inhumane."
The risk of harmful long-term effect or addiction is not relevant for them, he said.
But other doctors argue that newly available drugs do a better job of controlling the nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy than marijuana can.
And they say marijuana can cause unwanted effects, ranging from panic attacks to damage to the lungs.

"It's better than a placebo as an anti-emetic (anti-nausea), but not as good" as newer medications, Dr. Reese Jones of the University of California told the NIH panel, although he did support further research.
There are fewer studies on AIDS and marijuana, and most have used the synthetic THC pill.
